title: Starting a sourdough starter from flour and water
subtitle: How to build a live starter from scratch
excerpt: A sourdough starter is a live culture of wild yeast and bacteria grown in flour and water. Mix the two, feed daily, and within a week the culture becomes active enough to leaven bread. The starter is the foundation of every sourdough recipe.
sourceNotes: Technique developed from traditional European sourdough methods. Hydration ratios and flour choices draw from standard home-baking sourdough literature. The equal-weight flour-and-water approach (100% hydration) is the most widely taught starting point for beginners.

glossaryTerms.definition: A live culture of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria maintained in flour and water. The culture leavens bread and gives sourdough its distinctive flavour.
Naturally occurring yeast present on flour and in the surrounding environment, as distinct from commercial dried or fresh yeast.
A grey or brown liquid that forms on top of a neglected starter. It is alcohol produced by the culture and a sign the starter is hungry. Stir it back in or pour it off before feeding.

and bacteria colonise the mix. Once active, it leavens bread and gives sourdough its sour, open crumb. Building one takes about seven days of daily feeding.

Strong white bread flour and water. Whole-wheat or rye flour speeds colonisation because it carries more wild yeast. A clean glass jar with a loose-fitting lid works well; it lets gas escape without drying out the culture.

Mix 50 g strong white flour with 50 g water at room temperature (around 21°C). The consistency is thick porridge. Stir well, cover loosely, and leave at room temperature. Nothing will happen for the first day or two.

Discard half the starter (about 50 g). Add 50 g fresh flour and 50 g water. Stir, cover, leave. Repeat this once a day. The discard keeps the acid levels manageable and prevents the jar from becoming impossibly large. Use the discard in pancakes, crackers, or flatbreads.
By days 3 or 4 you should see small bubbles through the glass and the starter rising slightly between feeds. A sour, slightly fruity smell means fermentation is underway.

Continue the daily discard-and-feed. By day 5, the starter should double in size between feedings and show vigorous bubbling. Mark the side of the jar with a rubber band at feeding time to track the rise. A starter that doubles within 4 to 8 hours of a feeding is ready to bake with.
If the surface shows a thin grey liquid, that is

. Stir it back in and feed immediately. Cold kitchens (below 18°C) slow the culture; move the jar to a warmer spot or extend the timeline by a day or two. If there is no activity by day 4, try replacing some of the white flour with rye or whole-wheat flour.

A starter kept at 21 to 24°C is most predictable. Below 18°C the culture slows; above 30°C it can over-ferment and develop a vinegary edge. An oven with just the light on provides a steady 25°C in most kitchens.
